scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a policy response that backs strong wilderness laws while arguing 'any remaining' is too rigid; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Some of the last wild places on earth sit on land that companies would gladly develop.
One proposed policy is that nations should pass laws to preserve any remaining wilderness in its natural state, even where it could be developed for gain.
I strongly support protecting wilderness, but I believe a law covering every remaining area would be too rigid.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why preserving wilderness is vital

sentences.text: First, protecting wilderness by law brings deep and lasting benefits.
Wild areas shelter rare species and keep the natural systems we all rely on in balance.
For example, protected forests clean our air and water and guard plants found nowhere else.
This shows that preserving wilderness protects human life as much as nature.
Wild places also give people beauty, peace, and a rare sense of wonder.
Once developed, such land can almost never return to its natural state.
To this extent, strong laws to protect wilderness are clearly wise.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why an absolute rule is too rigid

sentences.text: Second, however, a law protecting every remaining area would be too rigid to be fair.
Some regions hold wild land that people urgently need for food, water, or shelter.
Consider a poor community whose only path out of poverty runs through a small part of its wild land.
Such cases show that an absolute ban could trap people in hardship for the sake of untouched land.
Carefully chosen limits can protect most wilderness while still meeting genuine human needs.
A rule covering every area ignores the real differences between places and situations.
Protection, then, should be strong but flexible rather than absolute.
In conclusion, nations should pass strong laws to protect their remaining wilderness.
But a rule preserving every area without exception would be too rigid and unfair.
The wisest laws guard most wilderness while leaving room for the most pressing human needs.
